tagline: Through the canyon country the Ancestral Puebloans left behind.
intro: Out of Cortez the road runs north by Dolores and then west on county roads, some of them gravel, toward Hovenweep, where six groups of Ancestral Puebloan villages stand on the Cajon Mesa, astride the Utah line. The Ancestral Puebloans held this canyon country from about AD 1 to 1300. They left cliff dwellings, rock art and pottery sherds, and kept most of their secrets.

In Utah the byway comes down to Bluff, settled in 1880 by Mormon families who had cut some 200 miles of their own trail to get there. From Mexican Hat it climbs onto Cedar Mesa toward Natural Bridges and swings back by way of Blanding.

moments.title: Yucca House
moments.text: At the foot of Sleeping Ute Mountain lies an unexcavated pueblo of up to 600 rooms and 100 kivas, its ruins 12 to 15 feet high and covered in vegetation.

moments.title: Moki Dugway
moments.text: North of Mexican Hat the pavement quits and SR 261 switchbacks up onto Cedar Mesa, on a road a mining company cut in 1958 to bring uranium ore down to the mill.

moments.title: Natural Bridges National Monument
moments.text: Three bridges with Hopi names, carved from white sandstone where White and Armstrong canyons meet. A gold prospector came on them in 1883, and they became Utah's first national monument.

practical: Some roads are gravel or native surface, muddy when wet, and a few call for stiff suspension or high clearance. The Moki Dugway on SR 261 is unpaved. In stormy weather ask locally about road conditions.
